citation: Early Chicago: Reception to the Settlers of Chicago Prior to 1840, by the Calumet Club, of Chicago, Tuesday Evening, May 27, 1879 (Chicago: Calumet Club, 1879) — the printed proceedings of the FIRST old-settlers' reception, with the registry of settlers who signed it.
author: The Calumet Club of Chicago
repository: Internet Archive, identifier earlychicagorece00calu (two further copies: cu31924028806707, earlychicagorecep00calu)
locator: the passage after the speeches: “of the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, one hundred and forty-nine registered their names out of the large number invited”, with the tables of “the places of birth, the years of arrival, and ages of those who signed the registry”
rights_note: Chicago, 1879: a United States imprint long out of copyright.
access_notes: READ, T-0577. The OCR text layer was read first, at the locator above: it is sound in the prose and MANGLED in the tables, so the register of pages 84-90 and the three aggregate tables of page 72 were read off the PAGE IMAGES instead — the item's own text PDF, rendered at 300 dpi and rotated upright, because the register is set sideways on the page. The transcription is committed at data/research/old_settlers/text/calumet_club_1879_registry.txt and the gate (tools/old_settlers.py --check) rebuilds every reading out of it. Note that the YEARS OF ARRIVAL table, previously recorded here as unreadable, is perfectly legible on the plate; only the OCR of it is destroyed.
what_it_supplies: the date, host and criterion of the first reception, 27 May 1879
the club's own count of 149 settlers who registered during the evening

the printed REGISTER itself, pages 84-90: 159 entries, each with the man's name, his own date of arrival in Chicago, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address — the only roster in the series that dates its people
the three aggregate tables of printed page 72 — places of birth, years of arrival and ages — each summing to 149, read off the plate rather than the OCR
what_it_does_not_supply: a residence in 1835. A date of arrival here is what the man said in 1879, forty to sixty years after the fact, and the club's criterion reaches to the end of 1839

which of the 159 printed entries are the 'few [who] called afterward and signed the registry' and are therefore outside the 149 the tables count — the plate does not mark them, and this project does not guess
an address in 1835: the register's fifth column is the 1879 post-office address
note: The one reception in the series whose roster dates its people, and the reason it was worth a run of its own. Read under T-0577.
